title: Calm Technology 02 — The People Behind the Idea

image.alt: A keyboard, small display, and speaker sit in a workspace with a pink curtain and mint pegboard, evoking computing distributed through objects and space.

slides.text:
One idea carried forward
by three people

Weiser and Brown framed the original problem. Amber Case later extended it into principles for contemporary product design and certification. Their roles differ, but their work forms a continuous line.

image.alt: A portrait of Mark Weiser, the Xerox PARC researcher who developed ubiquitous computing and helped establish the foundations of Calm Technology.

slides.text:
Mark Weiser asked where
computers should go next

Xerox PARC researcher Mark Weiser imagined ubiquitous computing: computers moving beyond a single screen and into objects and spaces.

If computers were everywhere, they could not demand our gaze every time they worked. The central question therefore became not only performance, but __what place technology should occupy in life__.

image.alt: A portrait of John Seely Brown, wearing glasses with gray hair and a beard. He co-authored the foundational Calm Technology papers with Mark Weiser.

slides.text:
John Seely Brown explained
the relationship alongside him

John Seely Brown co-authored “Designing Calm Technology” in 1995 and “The Coming Age of Calm Technology” in 1996 with Weiser.

The two texts presented Calm Technology not as a personal preference or simply ‘quiet design,’ but as __shared research into the relationship between people and technology__. It is most accurate to credit both men with the original proposal.

image.alt: Amber Case stands before a glass wall in a dark jacket and pink top. She brought Calm Technology principles into contemporary product design and certification.

slides.text:
Amber Case translated the research
for today's world

Designer and researcher Amber Case encountered PARC's Calm Technology work while writing an iPhone paper in 2007. She began speaking about it in 2010, published principles and a website in 2014, and later expanded the work through books for the IoT era.

She was not the original proposer. She became __the key figure who recovered the idea and turned it into applicable criteria__.

image.alt:
Eight principles begin with
the human state, not the device

slides.text:
Eight principles begin with
the human state, not the device

The Calm Tech Institute begins with the minimum amount of attention, ways to inform while creating calm, and use of the periphery. The remaining principles combine the strengths of humans and machines, communicate without speaking, continue through failure, use the minimum technology needed, and respect social norms.

The measure is not feature count, but __the burden a product leaves in people's lives and the agency it preserves__.

image.alt:
In 2024, the principles became
a product evaluation system

slides.text:
In 2024, the principles became
a product evaluation system

Amber Case launched the Calm Tech Institute in 2024 and introduced Calm Tech Certified™ that year. Products are assessed against 81-point criteria; public scorecards identify attention, periphery, durability, light, sound, and materials as core areas.

A research question had become __a practical language__ for reviewing and improving products.

image.alt:
If we asked first about the __relationship__
a technology creates with us,
what choices would change?

slides.text:
If we asked first about the __relationship__
a technology creates with us,
what choices would change?

caption.body: Calm Technology is not one person's slogan. Mark Weiser and John Seely Brown described how humans and technology might relate in an age of ubiquitous computing. Amber Case later translated that research into contemporary design principles and a certification system. Distinguishing the origin from the modern expansion makes the history of the idea clearer.
caption.cta: What choices would change if we asked first about the relationship a technology creates with us?
